The "la" Future Tense
The Immediate Future
The "la" future seems to have four principal uses.
1. An immediate future:
Aleta buleano. - He will come right now.
2. Expressing faith, giving a promise. This implies a greater definiteness, a greater certainty of coming to pass than other future tenses.
3. In the subjunctive mood, sometimes called "the remote future". This form is used in giving commands, asking for permission or instruction, with enya, lekha, and when referring to a specific time, or svat, to take place, at the future.
Inyanya yeyo dlelatsa. - On that day you will come?
4. In giving commands or instructions which are to be followed regularly as of this time onward.
Buli muviika mualitsanga ipasaka yino. - Every year you are to eat this passover.
Type A subject prefixes are used with the "la" future except for 1st person singular, "I" which uses only n- as subject prefix. The la is spoken on a relatively low tone. Since this cannot be shown in writing, a reduplicated form la is used with 1st person singular to differentiate in writing between the la future and the far past. The far past is spoken on a relatively high tone.
Ndalatsia buleano. - I shall go right away.
Pattern: Type A SF + la + VA + a/aga/njis/itsanga
Khulakhooya buleano. - We shall help right away.
Alabahu. - He will be here. (no stem is used in this tense)

Relative Construction with the La Future
1.Direct relative construction.
Positive:
Pattern: Type A DRP + la + VR + a/anga/njia/itsanga
Uno nye oulatzia bulasano. - This is the one who will go now.
Negative:
Pattern: Type A DRP + ra + VR + a/anga/njia/itsanga + ta/tawe
Ourakhoonya ta, ngowunuda. - This is the one who will not help.
2.Indirect relative construction.
Positive:
Pattern: IRP + (Subject) + Type A SP + VR + a/anga etc.
Omundu,owa alakhoonya,nomushiele uno. - The person whom he will help is this old women.
Negative:
Pattern: IRP + (Subject) + Type A SP + ra + VR + a/anga + ta
Omundu, owa . arakhoonya ta, nomusianu uyo. - The person whom he will not help is that boy.

Summary of khwo
We have studied numerous uses. The following introduces some other uses in a summary of all uses.
1.As a locative suffix: up, on, at, to, from on/at, etc.
Imeesa njevilia: niinskhwo. - There is the table yonder; climb up on it.
2.An absolute pronoun for class 9, the infinitive class.
Okhunaae yikhwo nikhwo okhulayi. - That sewing is that which is best.
3.Absolute pronoun for locative class 11.
Khundulo khuno nikhwo okhunyelele. - This on-the-edge place is the narrowest.
4.As possessive adjectives for classes 9 and 11.
Okhulukhwo nokhulayi pod. - Your weaving is very good!
Khundulokhwo nokhunyelele. - Your on-the-edge place is narrow.
5.For modifying the usual meaning of verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and sometimes even of nouns, usually in a diminutive sense.
Bukulakhwo. - Take some.
Endikhwo omulammi. - I am fairly well.
Khuleikhwo. - Let us eat a bite.
Olimile tulasyikhwo. - You dug fairly well.
Khunchonyilekhwo. - We are a little tired.
Balijo abanda balalakhwo. - There a few people here.
6.With the far past and present tenses, either simple or continuous. With positive construction it can mean "ever," and with negative construction, "never:"
Otsiitsangakhwo Nakuru? Bo, enziakhwo. - Do you ever go to Nakuru? Yes, I go there sometimes.
Wahulisikhwo khukabalulu bakhale? - Did you ever hear about the warriors of long ago?
Shindatsiakhwo Uganda tawe. - I have never gone to Uganda.
7.To mean "about."
Wahulile khukabandu bakhale? Tawe, shindahulilekhwo ta. - Did you hear about the people of long ago? No, I did not hear about them.
Amanyakhano keetsi leelo, ne omundi aboolangakhwo. - Difficulties came today, and the man is talking about them.
8.To intensify the effect of a negative verb.
Shinduutsikhwo ta. - I did not see at all.
Shikhuchamilekhwo ta. - We were not a bit pleased.
9.Two khwo's used as suffixes to the same verb, expressing two meanings. Or another locative suffix may be added.
Wahulile khukomulwele? Ndehulilekhvokhwo. - Have you heard about the sick person? I have heard a little about (him).
Nairobi relitookho lilayi; wamenyakhwoyo. - Nairobi is a nice city; have you ever lived there?
10.To express "from."
Khuisie Khureme emisakusa, khukasie khwo emisweselo. - Let us go cut some banana stalks and make sleds from them.

Neuter Verbs

This is a derived form of the verb. It indicates an intransitive state or condition, without any special reference to an agent which determines that state or condition. Often they are the equivalents of English words ending in "-able" and "-ible." Other times the idea is "get" or "become." The passive form of the verb indicates an agent which brings about the action. This neuter form indicates the action being done with no indication of an agent.

1.If the ultimate vowel of the root is a, i, or u.
Pattern: VR + ikha
manyikha - become well-known

2.If the ultimate vowel of the root is e or o.
Pattern: VR + ekha

(1) Corresponding to English -able and -ible

|-----------|---------|-------------|---------|

| hulli-    | hear, understand | hullikha | be audible/understandable |
| soom-     | read     | soomekha | be legible/readable |
| bool-     | say, speak, talk | boolekha | be pronounceable/sayable |
| khay-     | refuse   | khayikha | be intractable/refuse |
| chink-    | carry    | chinkikha | be portable/carriable |
| loi-      | see      | lolekha | be visible, appear |
| nyool-    | get, find, receive | nyolekha | be obtainable/findable |

As......as
In expressing "as much as," "as tall as," "as far as," etc., okuhuela is used in stating to what degree. Okuhelana na-/nende/nina- is used when comparing two or more objects as being equal to each other. Okuhela is also used for being worthy, and okuhela or okuhelana is used for expressing having as much right as another.

Relative Construction in the Near Future
1.Person class singular with consonants. (positive construction)
Pattern: Type A or B DRP + n + o + VR + e
Uno niye owanotsie. - This is the one who will go.
Uno niye owanotsie. - This is the one who will go.
Person class with vowels.
Pattern: Type A or B DRP + na + u + VR + e.
Ulia niye owansaule. - That one yonder is the one who will arrive.
2.All others.
Pattern: Type B DRP + na + Type A DRP minus IV + VR + e
Omulimo kuno nikwo okwanakukholve. - This is the work which will be done.
3.Negative construction.
Pattern: Type A DRP + ra + VR + e+ ta/tawe
Uno niye ouratsie ta. - This is the one who will not go.

Adjectival Expressions
There are few pure adjectives in Luyia, but many ways of expressing their equivalents in other languages. When standing alone, an adjec-

tive can be used as a noun and still retain its adjectival nature.
That is why they are called noun-adjectives.
1.Pattern: Ad.P + Ad.S
-lunjĩ - straight = omulunjĩ - straight person,
-nyełe - narrow, fine = ᵃⁿjĩlĩ ᵃⁿyełe - narrow path.
2.Pattern: PP + noun/adverb/infinite, etc.
omundi weshinani - a persevering/industrious person
Omukristayo watoto - a true Christian
ebindu ebiokhukusia - things to sell
3.Pattern: Ad.P + passive VS
-laamĩlĩ - heir = ᵃᵐusiānĩ ᵃᵐulaamĩlĩ - a son heir
-lekhwa - left one = ᵃᵐukhāsĩ ᵃᵐulekhwā - a widow; ᵃᵐwana ᵃᵐu-
-lingwa - foolish,silly = ᵃᵐbusĩ ᵃⁿyĩŋwā - a silly goat
4.Pattern: Ad.P + VR + s
-ahule - set apart,consecrate(for special purpose) = ᵃⁿgokho
-inzahule - a chicken set aside for a special purpose.
-lwale - sick, ill = ᵃⁿshĩmœmœ ᵃⁿshĩlwale - a sick lamb/kid
-teeshe - cooked,boiled = ᵃᵐatsĩ ᵃᵐateeshe - boiled water
-bohe - bound one,prisoner = ᵃᵐbusĩ ᵃⁿbohe - the tied goat
-kunze - artificial,something made = ᵃᵇĩmũ ᵃᵇĩkunze - artificial
flowers
5.Relative clause, particularly with neuter verbs.
ebindu ebinyooolekhanga - obtainable things
ingubo evipasajishe - an ironed dress
omundi owamanyikha - a well-known person
6.Ad.P + VR + u
tĩnyĩ - be hard,firm = ᵃⁿtĩnyĩ - hard firm,stubborn
-lihuka litĩnyĩ - a difficult word
mwamũ - become dark/black/dirty = ᵃⁿwamũ - dark,black,dirty
fuuhi - get dull/blunt. = ᵃⁿfuuhi - dull, blunt
tundũmũ - become warm = ᵃⁿtundũmũ - warm
umsũ - become dry/hard/stiff = ᵃⁿumsũ - dry, hard, stiff
yĩĩ - get hot;cook done = ᵃⁿyĩĩ - warm,fresh (milk)
7.Verbs ending in -era, -la, -na, -ba, etc. drop these endings and
add -fu, -sfu, or -ifu. Sometimes -ifu may be suffixed to VR.
sangalĩ - be happy/glad = ᵃⁿsangalĩ - happy, glad
tsatsahalĩ - be merry/glad = ᵃⁿtsatsahalĩ - merry, glad
tora - become thin/weak = ᵃⁿtofũ - weak (in character),
lazy
nyĩra - get cold/wet = ᵃⁿnyĩra - cool,cold,wet
bambalĩ,bambalĩ - spread out = ᵃⁿbambalĩfũ,(bambukhũ) - wide
labĩ - become white/clean/ = ᵃⁿlabĩ - white,light,clean
clear/mature
Special mention should be made of the -ndĩ (certain,other,some)
stem. When following a noun, it means "some,certain one(s),other(s)."
When it precedes the noun, it means a different type.

Exercise 6
Kalukhasia muLuluyia:
1.That is a right person. 2.The hail will spoil the gardens. 3.People of long ago experienced famines over and over. 4.John is the middle child of those three. 5.Peter is a strong and merciful person. 6.Words easily spoken are the ones which children should be taught. 7.A faithful person is one who ought to do right always. 8.Many things which are eaten do not give people strength. 9.A widow is a woman whose husband has died. 10.A foolish person is a person-who is not wise. 11.A messenger (sent one) is a person who is sent by another. 12.A citizen is an owner of the country in which he was born. 13.I shall drink cold water. 14.The children will drink fresh milk (freshly milked and still warm).
Questions
1.Word order is the same as in a statement of fact, with voice inflection for a question. The voice may begin on a relatively low tone, gradually rising to a high tone just before the last syllable at which time it drops to a low tone. Or the tone may begin low and rise higher ending on the highest pitch. Tone is important.
Oli omulamu? - Are you (s.) well?
Atsifile heena? - Where did he go?
2.When a negative question is asked, if the statement is true, the answer is, "Ee." If the statement is untrue, the Muluyia will state the matter as it is.
Abacheni shibatsiile ta? Ee. - The guests haven't gone? Yes
(meaning, that's right; they haven't gone).
Abacheni shibatsiile ta? Batsile. - The guests haven't gone? They have gone.
3.Ways of showing one is asking a question: by adding noho?, ta?, mba?, nohomba?, shikali kario (mbwo)?, and by voice inflection.
Abandu abashila obunj nabalasy. Shikali kario? - Most people are good. Aren't they?
Oli omulamu, nohomba? - You are well, aren't you?
4.Two kinds of negative questions.
a.The straightforward shi......tawe.
Shialihof ta. - He is not here.
b.When "yes" is the expected answer: shi...... (no ts/tawe)
Ne, shialihof? - But isn't he here? (You can see for yourself that he is).
Note that this type is often introduced by me.
5.Uses of ni and nina in questions. Niina may be used politely in appealing to reason, or it may be rude, depending on the tone of voice used. Ni seems to be a rude form. Often a vocative (mama, bandu, beefwe, etc.) is used to enhance politeness.
Ohokolanga shina? Ne, shindeekanga ni? - What are you doing?
Can't you see perfectly well that I am cooking?

Shinzeyile niina? 6.O! shmutzisile? Be, khushiliko. 7.Ne omulwale uyo shjahonile ta? Be, 8.Shimuleerile omwana tawe? Be, ali ingo. 9.Abekaana shibali-mile leelo ta? Balimile. 10.O! muliho! A! ta! khushili! 11.O! witsile-1e? A-a! eshilli. (These last two are used in fun). 12.Reebe uyo li-reebo lianjie. 13.E! iwe shioreebile ta? Eshili. 13.Leya, wosiye teisa-haani? Ne, shinzosiye niina, Mama? (This answer would be gentle).

Equivalent of English Relative Pronouns
This treats of such statements as, He wants to know when you will go; "he is asking where they are going," etc. The more common way in Luyia is to use the interrogative pronouns, liina? heena? etc.

Ne shiyamboolee ta.3.Ereebile Sara natsie arie Eshisumu, nyiamboolela mbu natsiile mutekesi.4.Papa yeenyä okhumanya Yohana arullile hano liina.5.Kwamuboleele eshifurwe eshiachilile nikhwenyä okuhima omukunda.6.Areebanga kutsiile liina, khandi khukaluushe liina.
A less common way for these sentences is relative construction:
1.Yohana yeenyä okhumanya olwa notsie Mwihila.2.Enduutsi Leya kuhnjila, nimureeba aha atsitsanga.3.Ereebile Sara shinge olwa natsie Eshisumu.4.Papa yeenyä okhumanya olwa Yohana arullile hano.6.Areebanga olwa khutsiile, khandi olwa khukaluushe.

But she did not tell me.3.I asked Sarah how she is going to Kisumu, and she told me that she is going in a taxi.4.Father wants to know when John left here.5.We told him why we wanted to dig in the garden.6.She is asking when we went, and when we returned.
Reversive Forms of Verbs
This form expresses the reverse or contrary action of that expressed in the original verb form. It has two forms, transitive and intransitive.
1.Verbs whose ultimate vowel in the root is a, e, i, or u:
Pattern: VR + ula/ulule/ula (transitive)
Pattern: VR + ulukha/ululukha (intransitive)
2.Verbs whose ultimate vowel in the root is o:
Pattern: VR + ola/olola/ola (transitive)
In this last ending it seems that the first l has been elided.
Pattern: VR + okha/olokha (intransitive)

2.The Impossible Contingent.
This is practically the equivalent of the English past perfect
tense of the subjunctive mood: If I had been guilty, I would have
confessed; If He had gone, he would have enjoyed the play; Had I
seen her, I would have spoken, etc.
In the impossible contingent there is an "if" clause and a main,
or contingent, clause.
a.The "if" clause. (positives)
Pattern: Type A SP + la + ba + ni + Type B SP + kha + VS in past
Claba niwakhabeele ingo - If you had been at home.
(tense)
(negative)
Pattern: Type A SP + la + ba + ni + Type A SP + raa + VS in past
tense + ta
Ingokho yilebe niyiraakonela amabuyu ta - If the chicken has
not sat on the eggs.
The ni may be omitted from the second verb:
Ingokho yilabe yiraskonela amabuyu ta.
b.The contingent (main) clause. (near past tense)
Pattern: khane + (subject *) Type B SP + kha + VS in near past
tense
Khane khwakhasikaale hano. - We would have remained here.
The form just given is for the near past tense. A variation of
this would be: Khane khuskikaale hano. - We would have remained
here. Another variation: omit the khane and use the near past
verb with Type B SP + kha + VS in near past tense.
Khwakhasikaale hano. - We would have remained here.
This last form is used more than any other in near past tenses.

The main clause in other past tenses:
Pattern: khane + Type B SP + VS in immediate/intermediate/far past tense
Khane ndakhatsia. - I would just now have gone.
Khane ndatsiile. - I would have gone (sometime during the past four or five days).
Khane ndatsia. - I would have gone (long ago).
This clause uses the shi...tave negative.
c.There are variations of the "if" clause.
(1) full clause:
Olaba niwakhabeela ingo - If you had been at home.
(2) 1st variation:
Niwakhabeele ingo - If you had been at home.
(3) 2nd variation:
Wakhabeele ingo - If you had been at home.
(4) 3rd variation:
Niwabeele ingo - If you had been at home.
(5) 4th variation:
Olaba wakhabeele ingo - If you had been at home.
(6) 5th variation:
Olaba wabeel ingo - If you had been at home.
One of these three must be present: laba, or ni, or kha; all may be present, or two may be present in any combination. It is suggested that the student learn the full form first, then take up the variations at his convenience.

Adverbs
There are three kinds of adverbs: (1) adverbs of time, (2) adverbs of place, (3) adverbs of manner. There are very few primitive adverbs; most all are composed of an adverbial prefix, which in adverbs of time and manner are usually the same as the adjective prefix minus the initial vowel, plus the adverb stem. Nearly all adverbs of place 1 are locative nouns from the locative-noun-classes. When the word "of" is needed with them, the possessive particle of class 14, wa-, is used: imbeli wa- - in front of.
Some of the Baluyu retain the initial vowel in the adverb prefix, Akholie obulayi. - He did well; but most drop the initial vowel, Akholie bulayi.
Many adverbs of place are also used as adverbs of time: habwenaho - that same place, immediately, etc. A list of adverbs is given below.
1. Adverbs of Time.
obushia - day-after-tomorrow
ahambili hano, aheembichiti hano - recently (with past tense); soon (with future tense)
tsuli - early (in the morning)
khatsotsso, khacsotsso, khatsotsotso - always, regularly, repeatedly
khale - long ago, early (ahead of time)
mukamba, mutsuli - in the morning
mukolooba, olwabelee - yesterday
mubwile, mushitsizambo, khubwile - in the afternoon
mushiteere, mumbasu - in the daytime
olunyuma - afterwards
olunyumakhwo - a little later.
olunyuma wayako, inyuma wayako - after that
olwambeli, olwokhuranga - at first
2. Adverbs of Place.
indulo wa- - the side of
khundulo wa- - at the side of, along the edge
imbeli - in front; imbeli wa- - in front of
inyuma - behind; inyuma wa- - back of, after
munyuma wa- - in the/at the back of
halubeka, elubeka - at the side, to one side
halala - together (from -lala, stem for number 1 = at one place)
hakari - in the middle; hakari wa- - between; mukari - inside
eshilihwa - front entrance; hashilihwa - at the front entrance
ehale - far away, away
habwenaho, habwenye yaho - at that very place, immediately
ebweneyo, ebwenye yiyo - at that very place (class 14)
emwalo - down the slope (farther down than where the speaker is)
mulwalo - down at the bottom
hekulu - above, up, the place above (not very high)
indengu - behind the house
emukulu - up the slope (farther on up)
elwanyi - outside.
hasi - down, below, on the floor
3. Adverbs of Manner.
a. using adverbial prefixes bu-, lu-, ha-, shi-.
shilunjĩ, buhesikhu - clearly, distinctly, right out
luhunzo - on the side
lukano - differently, variously
habulafu, ebulafu - openly, publicly, in the light
kalaha - slowly, softly, carefully
bwangu - quickly, lightly, easily

Persistive Verbs
The main idea of these verbs seems to be a concentrated persistence
and augmentation of meaning. There are dialect differences of meaning.
1.Verbs whose ultimate root vowel is a, i, or u.
Pattern: VR + ilila
ching + ilila = chinjilila - carry many little things from one
place to another, as gossipy words
2.Verbs whose ultimate root vowel is e, or o.
Pattern: VR + elela
nyool + elela = nyoolielela - catch in the act
3.Monosyllabic verbs.
Group a:
Pattern: VS + ilelela (coalesce)
hwa + ilelela = hweelelela
Group b:
Pattern: VR + ililila
tsi + ililila = tsililila
Original Verb Persistent Verb
lwal - be ill lwallilila - be recurrently ill
teekha - cook teesheelela - cook for a long period of time
londaka - follow on londachilile - follow until one overtakes
male - finish melilila (one elided) - finish off
linda - wait lindilila - wait and wait (on)

sambu - burn sambilila - weld, solder, burn through
henga - look henjelila - spy on, watch secretly
khama - disappear, squeeze khamilila - gradually disappear, squeeze much
sinjila - stand sinjilila - have oversight of/be overseer
hwa - come to end hweelelela - languish, gradually weaken/end

Interjections
There are three kinds of interjections: (1) primitive, (2)vocative,
and (3) imperative.
1.Primitive interjections.
These have some of the characteristics of ideophones. They are
highly emotional. Here are some.
koo! - Mind! Listen! or kokoko! - Listen! Pay attention.
yakoomba! - Here now, none of that! (reproof, refusal)
khane! - Of all things! What do you know!
ma! or ma!ma!ma! - Oh,goody,goody! (surprised amazement)
wale! or wole! - See! I told you so!
ta! - No! Not really! Is that so! (disbelief and amazement)
atsa! - Here,here, none of that! (disgust)
tieri! - Quite true! It is a fact!
apopo! - Careful there!
apo! - Not at all! (complete denial)
awa! - Not a bit of it! (dissavowal and disgust)
bulayi! - wonderful!
mako! - Goody,goody! That's simply wonderful!
2.Vocatives.
These are person class nouns and pronouns from which the initial
vowel, if there is one, has been elided.
bene! - My goodness! Good gracious! or Too bad!
bandu! - These first five are mostly expressions of surprise or
beefwe! - merely to get attention.
bandu beefwe! - well I'm bothered!
mwe! -
baena! -
bakhasi! - used when danger is apparent
bayaye! (from omuyaye - boy) - expresses dismay,a sense of catastrophe
, sorrow, or indignation - real or feigned.
3.Imperatives.
The tone of voice will determine whether the imperative is an in
terjection or not. Only a few are listed below.
tsia! tsia! - get going!
hwaho! - be gone with you!
tsia bwangu! - go quickly!
tsia bwangu, koo! - go quickly, hear!
lekhai! - stop!

Ni Construction of Verbs
Compound verb forms are expressed very often by the verb "to be" in
combination with ni construction.
The ra...tawe negative is used with all verbs in ni construction.
1.Showing two or more actions going on simultaneously, both during
the same time period.
Pattern: olwa + SP + VS of verb "to be" in proper tense + ni + Type A
SP + VS in present tense continuous (dependent clause)
Olwa khube nikhutsiitsanga - While we are going.
Olwa khubele nikhutsiitsange - While we were going.
Note that in the present tense the verb "to be" uses the ba stem
in this form. All other tenses use the usual forms.
Olwa nakhube nikhutsiitsanga - While we shall be going.
The main olawa is the same as the dependent, or "while," except
that olwa is omitted. The verb "to be" sets the tense and the verb
in ni construction is in the present tense continuous. A sample
sentence given below demonstrates this.
Olwa uno aba nalilitsanga, uyo aba nateekhanga. - While this one
is eating, that one is cooking.
Olwa uno yakhaba nalilitsanga, uyo yakhaba nateekhanga. - While
this one was just now eating, that one was just now cooking.
Olwa uno abeele nalilitsanga, uyo abeele nateekhanga. - While
this one was eating, that one was cooking (today).
Olwa uno yabeele nalilitsanga, uyo yabeele nateekhanga. - While
this one was eating, that one was cooking (yesterday).
Olwa uno yali nalilitsanga, uyo yali nateekhanga. - While this
one was eating, that one was cooking (long ago).
Olwa uno nabe nalilitsanga, uyo nabe nateekhanga. - While this
one will be eating, that one will be cooking.
Olwa uno yakhaba nalilitsanga, uyo yakhaba nateekhanga. - While

2.Showing a single act taking place while another action is in the
process of being done.
Pattern:(olwa +)SP + VS of "to be" in proper tense + ni + Type A
SP + VS in present continuous (action in progress clause)
Olwa yali nachendelanga mumutoka - While he was travelling in
the car.
or
Yali nachendelanga mumutoka, olwa - He was travelling in the car
when, etc.
Pattern:(olwa +) SP + VR + tense ending (single act clause)
(Olwa) yalola omusaakhulu. -(When) he saw the old man.
Sample sentence:
Olwa khubeele nikhuremulanga, khuluutsi inzokha. - While we were
clearing, we saw a snake.
Khwabeele nikhuremulanga olwa khweluutsei inzokha. - We were clearing
off (weeds, etc.) when we saw a snake.
The verb "to be" form may be omitted and only the ni verb used.
Note that olwa with the clause showing the action in progress is interpreted as "while," and in the clause showing a single act, "when."

3.Relative clauses in this form.
This is used very little and need only be mentioned. This form is
used in giving a reason why one does or does not do a thing.
Nireetsa tawe, emilino echia emba nikholangane minijji. - If I
do not come,(it is because) the work which I am doing is too
much.
Nireayinzilanga bulayi ta, emilino echia emba nikholangane chimbiyiile. - If I am not working well,(it is because) the work which
I am doing has become distasteful to me.
4.Consecutive Construction.
In Luyis this may refer either to past or future tenses. The main
verb sets the tense, and other verbs of narration are in ni
construction in present tense form. The verb "to be" in past tense
consecutive construction uses the ba stem: nikaba, niliba, etc.
Pattern: ni + Type A SP + VS in present tense, usually simple

8.Past Perfect Tense.
Although this tense in Luyia has the basic idea of relationship of one period with another, the equivalent of the English past perfect tense is also expressed in these forms.
The English past perfect is formed by "had" + past participle: He had gone. Luyia uses the verb "to be" (in place of "had") + the past participle. The verb "to be" is in the same tense as the verbs in the other clauses of the sentence, while the past participle indicates how long before that the action took place.
Pattern: SP + VS of "to be" agreeing in tense with other verbs + ni + SP + VS in past tense which indicates how long before
Sample sentence:
1.Olwa khuulileyo,shikhumunyoolile ta, shichila abeeli niyakhatsia.
abeele netsiile.
abeele niyatsiile.
abeele niyatsia.
When we arrived there (today),we did not find him, because
he had just gone,
he had gone (today).
he had gone (yesterday).
he had gone (long ago).
This same pattern is followed through with the verb "to be" and
and the other verbs in other tenses.

9.Future Perfect Tense.
In this tense the same basic pattern is followed as for the past perfect tense. All the verbs in ni construction behave in the same manner. But all other verbs are in a future tense.
Pattern: SP + VS of "to be" agreeing in future tense with verbs in the other clauses * ni + SP + VS in past tense showing how long before.

nabe niyatsiile.
nabe niyatsia kale.

he will have gone long before.

aliba natsiile.

alabe natsiile.

10. Until.
Pattern: okhuula olwa (more commonly used)
Balia okhuula olwa beekura. - They ate until they were satisfied.
Pattern: okhuula + ni + SP + VS (less common)
Batsile okhuula nibschoonyile. - They went until they were tired.
Past and future tenses of the verbs may be used, or verbs in the subjunctive mood, even the present tense is used.

kuno po! 9.Okhurulana omwana nakona, sshili okhusimukhuka (okhubukha
). 10.Okhurulana khukhuchaka kwheshielo abandu boonoonange.
Exercise 22
Kalukhasia muLuluyia:
1.It is two days today since he went to his village. 2.It is now
four years since we came to Kisumu. 3.From the time they left we
harvested potatoes. 4.Ever since our guests have come, we have been
cooking very much. 5.Ever since they finished their examinations,
they have just been sitting. 6.From Wednesday until today their
child (brother/sister) was ill. 7.Since the beginning of this month
we have not been receiving enough milk. 8.Since this morning until
now the cars have been passing back and forth very much on this road.
9.Ever since the child went to sleep, he has not yet awakened. 10.
Ever since the beginning of the world people have been sinning.
13.Already.
Pattern: SP + melile * infinitive,also in compound form with to ba
Amalile okhutsia. - She has already gone.
Exercise 23
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1.Ndatsia okhukula amapwoni, ne ndanyoola nikamalile okhuhwa. 2.
Khwenyile okhukula ambuyu, ne keli nikamalile okhukusiba. 3.Beenya
okhutsila Eshisumu mumutoka, nebutswa kweli nikamalile okhubalekha.
4.Khwenyile okhuniina mularo, nebutswa liakhomals okhutsia. 5.Mukolooba
ndetsile Khwiseelo okhulola Andanje, ne ndanyoolile mbu umalile
okhutsia ewabo. 6.Khwp.era okhurema amaramwa (amakomia) ne khwanyoola
kamalile okhuhwa.
